t: Flower Planting With No Adjacent — Greedy Graph Coloring in 4 Colors
o: We must color each garden with one of 4 flower types so that adjacent gardens differ. This is graph coloring on a graph where every vertex has degree at most 3. By Brooks' theorem / the greedy argument, any graph of maximum degree d is (d+1)-colorable: when we color a vertex, at most 3 neighbors already have colors, so one of 4 colors is always free. Example 1 is a triangle needing 3 distinct colors; example 2 has two disconnected edges so reusing colors across components is fine; example 3 is K4 requiring all 4 colors. The degree bound guarantees a valid answer always exists and makes a simple greedy pass sufficient — no backtracking needed.
k: Max degree ≤ 3 means any vertex conflicts with at most 3 neighbors, so among 4 flower types at least one is always available.
A single left-to-right greedy pass suffices: color each garden with the smallest type not used by its already-colored neighbors.
The garden labels are 1..n and map directly to array indices, so no coordinate compression is needed.

a.i: Process gardens in order 1..n. For each garden, collect the flower types used by its neighbors that were colored earlier, then pick any type from {1,2,3,4} not in that set. Since a garden has at most 3 neighbors total, at most 3 types are blocked, leaving at least one choice. Because later neighbors are colored after this one, they will avoid this garden's color by the same argument, so validity holds globally.
s: Build an adjacency list from paths.
Initialize answer array of size n with zeros.
For each garden i from 1 to n, gather colors of already-colored neighbors.
Assign the smallest color in 1..4 not used by those neighbors.
a.t: O(n + m) — building the adjacency list and scanning each garden's small neighbor list once.
a.sp: O(n + m) — adjacency list plus the answer array.

a.i: Same greedy principle, but traverse the graph component-by-component with DFS. At each node, mark neighbor colors as unavailable and pick a free color, then recurse into uncolored neighbors. This handles disconnected graphs naturally and is the pattern to reach for if the problem were generalized to arbitrary traversal order or online queries.
s: Build an adjacency list from paths.
For every uncolored garden, start a DFS.
In DFS, compute the set of colors used by neighbors and assign a free color.
a.t: O(n + m) — each vertex and edge is visited a constant number of times during DFS.
a.sp: O(n + m) — adjacency list plus recursion stack up to O(n) deep.

w: Prefer Approach 1 in an interview: it is iterative (no recursion-depth concerns), shorter, and the linear scan order trivially guarantees earlier neighbors are colored. Key pitfall: forgetting that the guarantee 'max degree ≤ 3' is what makes 4 colors provably enough — without it you would need backtracking or planarity arguments. Edge cases: n = 1 with no paths (answer [1]), disconnected components (handled naturally since unvisited nodes get their own pass), and duplicate handling of bidirectional edges (add both directions). Follow-ups might ask why 4 colors suffice (greedy/Brooks' theorem argument), whether 3 colors could work (no — K4 in example 3 needs 4), or how to minimize the number of distinct flowers used (NP-hard in general, but tractable here due to the structure).
